title: Zero divisors, cancellation, and integral domains
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Integral Domains
terms: zero divisor; left zero divisor; right zero divisor; integral domain; cancellation in a ring.

exposition.text:
A nonzero element is a zero divisor if it multiplies some nonzero element to zero; in a noncom-
mutative ring one distinguishes sides. An integral domain is a commutative unital ring with
1 ̸= 0 and no nonzero zero divisors. Thus ab = 0 forces a = 0 or b = 0, and multiplication by a
nonzero element can be canceled.
In Z , a nonzero class is a zero divisor exactly when it is not coprime to n; Z is a domain
n n
exactly when n is prime. A product of two nonzero rings is not a domain: for nonzero a, b in its
factors, (a, 0)(0, b) = 0. Matrix rings and unrestricted function rings supply many zero divisors,
even when their scalar coefficients lie in a field.
Here the side names follow the source: if ab = 0 with a, b ̸= 0, the left factor a is a left zero
divisor and the right factor b is a right zero divisor. Some texts reverse this terminology, so the
equation is decisive. Nonzero elements that are not zero divisors need not be units in an infinite
ring; multiplication by such an element can be injective without being surjective.

question.text:
How many nonzero zero divisors are in Z ?
45
(A) 12 (B) 20 (C) 21 (D) 24 (E) 30

solution.text:
There are φ(45) = 45(1 − 1/3)(1 − 1/5) = 24 units. Of the 44 nonzero classes, the remaining
44 − 24 = 20 are zero divisors.

question.text:

In an integral domain R, nonzero elements a, b satisfy a = b . Which conclusion always fol-
lows?
(A) a = b (B) a = −b (C) a = b or a = −b (D) a + b = 1 (E) a and b are units

solution.text:
Commutativity gives (a − b)(a + b) = 0. Since there are no nonzero zero divisors, one factor is
zero. One cannot simply cancel a factor of a against a factor of b. Both signs are possible,
for example in Z, and being a unit is unnecessary.

BLR = 0, so it is not a right zero divisor. A one-sided inverse in an infinite-dimensional
setting need not be two-sided.

question.text:
In C([0, 1], R) under pointwise operations, let f(x) = x. Which statement is correct?
(A) f is a unit.
(B) f is a nonzero zero divisor.
(C) f is neither a unit nor a zero divisor.
(D) f is nilpotent.
(E) f is idempotent.

solution.text:
It is not a unit because it vanishes at zero. If fg = 0 with g continuous, then g(x) = 0 for
every x > 0, and continuity also gives g(0) = 0. Thus multiplication by f is injective even
though f has no inverse in this ring. In infinite rings, a nonunit need not be a zero divisor.
